hint: Vaccinium and Gaylussacia both trade under the name; the Northwest's wild mountain huckleberry is never cultivated at scale. Distinguish from blueberry (the ten hard seeds of a true huckleberry against the soft seeds of a blueberry).
An Oregon blackberry cross (Chehalem x Olallie, released 1956), most of the state's crop; it is a blackberry, not a species of its own.
Rubus spectabilis, the Pacific Northwest's first berry of the year, salmon to red, watery and mild; a raspberry relative that hollows off the receptacle.
Amelanchier: saskatoon, juneberry, shadbush; a pome that eats like a blueberry with almond in the seed.
Crataegus haws: mealy, seedy, pectin-rich; jelly, haw flakes and tanghulu; the seeds carry amygdalin and are not eaten.
A 1920s California cross of blackberry, raspberry and loganberry; large, soft, wine-dark, sharp; too fragile to travel, so mostly frozen, jammed or in pie.
Rubus occidentalis, the Midwest's blackcap: hollow like a red raspberry, seedier, drier, deeply pigmented; not a blackberry.
Asimina triloba, North America's largest native fruit, custard flesh tasting of banana and mango; two-day shelf life; the skin and seeds are not eaten and some people react to the fruit.
Any Malus fruit under about 5 cm; high pectin and malic acid, so it sets jelly alone and pickles whole; astringent raw.
Vitis rotundifolia, the Southeast's native grape: thick slip skin, musky, large seeds, eaten by squeezing the pulp out; scuppernong is the bronze cultivar; jelly, hull pie and sweet wine.
Eriobotrya japonica, a spring pome from a rose-family evergreen: apricot-yellow, sweet-tart, two to four large seeds; bruises within a day; the seeds hold amygdalin.

Vigna unguiculata, the Southern pea: crowder, cream, purple hull and black-eyed are all cultivars; shelled fresh in summer and dried the rest of the year; cooked with a smoked cut. The Lexicon already has Black-eyed Pea; this entry is the family.

Phaseolus lunatus: the small green baby lima and the large cream butter bean are the same species; fresh-shelled in summer, dried or frozen otherwise; raw beans hold linamarin, so they are always cooked. MUST ANSWER (the 27 Sep refuters, safety): a ten minute boil settles the lectin, NOT the cyanide (heat kills linamarase and leaves linamarin in the seed); the cyanide goes out with the soak water, which is poured away, and a long uncovered cook in plenty of fresh water, also poured away; the prep must say drain. Dried beans keep two or three years cool and dry: warmth and damp, not the calendar, cause hard-to-cook. The large cream butter bean is confused in loose bins with the dried fava (vicine, favism in G6PD deficiency): give the tell (lima: plump half-moon, white eye, fine ridges fanning from it; fava: flatter, thick skinned, dark scar) and name FAVA BEAN. The ham hock goes in from the start, only the corn late.

The Mirasol-type chile of Pueblo, Colorado (Mosco is the named cultivar), thick-walled, fruit pointing up, roasted in drum roasters in September; hotter and meatier than Hatch; a Southwest regional rivalry a server will hear about.

Calvatia gigantea and its kin: eaten only while the interior is pure white and uniform throughout, sliced like bread and fried; a cut face showing any yellow, any gill outline or a developing stem means it is past, or is a young Amanita button, which kills. That check is the whole entry. MUST ANSWER (the 27 Sep refuters, safety): the gleba is the FERTILE spore-bearing tissue, white only while unripe (the sterile part is the subgleba at the base); halve EVERY specimen top to bottom and read each face, since a bag of small Lycoperdon is where an Amanita egg hides; the earthball (Scleroderma) is judged by its thick, hard, ochre-yellow, scaly rind, because very young it is white inside too; amatoxin poisoning is biphasic: symptoms six to twenty-four hours after the meal, a false recovery, then liver failure on day two to four.

Jamaican: allspice (pimento) and Scotch bonnet are the two fixed points, with thyme, scallion, garlic, ginger, brown sugar, nutmeg, cinnamon; a dry rub or a wet paste; traditionally cooked over pimento wood.

American chili powder is a BLEND (ground dried chiles with cumin, oregano, garlic, sometimes salt), invented in Texas for chili con carne; not the same as pure ground chile (chile powder, cayenne) and a common menu confusion.

Prosopis pods, the Southwest's native sweet legume: ground to a flour that tastes of caramel and cinnamon, used in baking and drinks; the same tree is the barbecue wood. The plate lists it among fruits; the entry says what a kitchen actually buys.
